778.title: Lateran IV, 1215
778.hook: the council uses the word transubstantiation and asks Catholics to confess and receive at least yearly
778.howItsDone: Catholic parishes post regular times for confession, and the precepts of the Church ask Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year and receive communion at least during the Easter season; Catholics may go far more often.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople, a city sacked by fellow Christians. Your line was sorrow, centuries later. Did an old apology come to mind? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

Where does the phrase Easter duty come from? Some Catholics still use it: the yearly confession and communion around Easter, the floor below which you don't go. It comes from a meeting of bishops in Rome, at the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral church. The same Pope Innocent from yesterday's story called it. Bishops and abbots came from across the West. They wrote decrees on all sorts of things, but two lines from that meeting are still part of ordinary Catholic life. Today's word is Lateran IV, the fourth council held there.
screen: `WHERE THE EASTER DUTY COMES FROM.` → `THE POPE'S CATHEDRAL.` → `TWO LINES THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: First line, about the altar. The council opens with a statement of faith, and in it, it says that in the Mass the bread and wine are transubstantiated by divine power into Christ's body and blood. That's the word transubstantiation, in a council's own text. The council didn't invent the belief. Catholics read it in Jesus' words in John's Gospel, which in the Douay-Rheims read: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." What the council did was give the belief a careful name: what the bread is changes, while what it looks like stays. Second line, about the heart. Another decree says that every one of the faithful, man or woman, once they reach the age of discretion, should confess their sins faithfully at least once a year to their own priest, and receive communion with reverence at least at Easter. Then, the surprise. Notice the words at least. This was never meant as the goal. It was a floor, a minimum for people who might otherwise drift for years. The council wasn't saying once a year is enough. It was saying, at the very least, don't go longer than this. Last, why it lasts. The Church still keeps both lines. Catholics call them precepts of the Church: confess serious sins at least once a year, and receive communion at least during the Easter season. Nothing stops a Catholic from going far more often. The floor is there for the years when life gets thin: at least once a year.
screen: `TRANSUBSTANTIATED: A CAREFUL NAME.` · `CONFESS AND RECEIVE, YEARLY.` · `A FLOOR, NOT A GOAL.` · `STILL A PRECEPT TODAY.` · then, large: `AT LEAST ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan your next confession, or, if confession isn't part of your life, plan your next honest look at yourself. Use the sit. First, think back: when was the last time? Don't judge the answer, just notice it. Then pick a real day and a place: a parish schedule you could check, a quiet evening you could set aside. Then let one or two things you'd want to bring rise to mind, without digging. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to keep the date. The bell holds the time.
Lateran IV. The fourth council at the Lateran in Rome, which named transubstantiation and set the yearly minimum for confession and Easter communion. Today's word.
Your line: at least once a year. Today, find one practice you've let slide below its floor, and put it back on a calendar. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Constance, 1414–1418
779.hook: three men claim to be pope, and a council ends the split
779.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the unity of the Church at Mass and in particular during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity; the Council of Constance is remembered as the council that ended the Western Schism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lateran IV, and the floor under Catholic practice. Your line was at least once a year. Did anything go back on the calendar? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

A parish priest in those years could honestly not be sure who the pope was. One man in Rome claimed the office. Another, in Avignon in southern France, claimed it too. Then a council at Pisa tried to fix things by electing a third, and the other two refused to step aside. Kingdoms lined up behind different men. It was a mess no one could pray their way out of alone. Today's word is Constance, the German lakeside town where the bishops finally met to end it.
screen: `WHO IS THE POPE?` → `ROME, AVIGNON, PISA.` → `A TOWN BY A LAKE.`

segments.voice: First, the knot. Each claimant had cardinals, bishops and rulers behind him. Each said the others were the false ones. Ordinary Catholics wanted one shepherd and couldn't find him. Then, the council gathers. The German king Sigismund pressed for it, and the claimant from the Pisa line called it. Bishops, abbots, theologians and princes came. When that claimant saw where things were going, he slipped out of town in disguise. He was brought back, and the council deposed him. Next, the man in Rome. Gregory the Twelfth did something rare. He allowed the council to be formally called in his name, and then he resigned. He let go of the office so the Church could have one pope. Catholic lists of the popes follow his line, and his resignation opened the door. The claimant in Avignon would not yield, and the council deposed him too, though he held out to the end with a few supporters. Then the council elected one man, who took the name Martin the Fifth, and the split was over. There's a hard shadow on this council, and it should be named: it also condemned the Czech preacher Jan Hus, who was burned at the stake. Pope John Paul the Second later spoke of deep regret over his death. Paul asks the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, to be "careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." At Constance, unity cost something. One man had to let go. Three popes, then one.
screen: `THE KNOT: THREE CLAIMANTS.` · `ONE FLEES AND IS DEPOSED.` · `ONE RESIGNS FOR UNITY.` · `ONE ELECTED: MARTIN V.` · then, large: `THREE POPES, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for unity in the Church, or, if you don't pray, hold it in mind. Use the sit. Bring to mind one split you know of: in a parish, a family, a group of friends, between churches. Don't decide who's right. Just hold both sides in view for a few breaths. Then ask yourself what one person would need to let go of for the knot to loosen, and whether that person could be you. If you pray, you can ask for the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The bell holds the time.
Constance. The council in a German lakeside town that ended the split of rival popes, with one resignation, two depositions and one election. Today's word.
Your line: three popes, then one. Today, in one small quarrel, try letting go of being right so that something whole can come back. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: Florence, 1439
780.hook: East and West sign a reunion that doesn't last
780.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches continue formal theological dialogue today, and their leaders meet and pray together; the Council of Florence is remembered by Catholics as a reunion that was signed but not received in the East.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constance, where the West's split was finally healed. Your line was three popes, then one. Today the council looks east, to the older wound. Day seven hundred eighty.

"Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad." That's a line from the Psalms. It's also how a decree begins, read aloud in the cathedral of Florence, in Latin and in Greek, with the Eastern emperor present and bishops of East and West standing in the same church. Its first words in Latin, laetentur caeli, became its name. After the schism, after the sack of Constantinople, East and West had signed their names to being one Church again. Today's word is Florence. And today's story is about how close they came.
screen: `LET THE HEAVENS REJOICE.` → `LATIN AND GREEK, ONE CHURCH.` → `HOW CLOSE THEY CAME.`

segments.voice: First, the long talks. The Greeks came west, emperor and bishops together, partly because their city was in danger and they hoped for help. But they didn't come only for help. At length, theologians argued in earnest over the old questions: how the Holy Spirit proceeds, what happens to souls after death, the authority of the pope, even whether the bread of the Mass should be leavened or unleavened. Then, the agreement. The decree tried to show that the two sides often meant the same truth in different words. On the bread, it said both customs were valid: the Latins could keep theirs and the Greeks theirs. It's a careful, generous document. Next, the one who wouldn't sign. Mark, the bishop of Ephesus, refused. He was sure the agreement gave away too much. Orthodox Christians honor him as a saint for standing firm. Catholics remember the council as a real reunion that was not received. Finally, the homecoming. When the delegates went back east, clergy and people refused what had been signed. The union never took hold, and after a while it was set aside. On paper they were one. In the parishes, they were not. Almost one. It isn't a story of failure only. Florence showed that East and West could sit at one table, pray in one church, and find shared words. That is worth remembering whenever the two churches talk today.
screen: `LONG, HONEST ARGUMENT.` · `SAME TRUTH, DIFFERENT WORDS.` · `ONE BISHOP REFUSES.` · `SIGNED, BUT NOT RECEIVED.` · then, large: `ALMOST ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep trying at a hard reconciliation. Bring to mind one you've already tried, maybe more than once, that didn't hold. A friend, a sibling, a parent, an old colleague. For the sit, don't replay the fight. Notice what you did agree on, even if it was small. Then picture one next step, the smallest one that wouldn't cost your honesty: a message, a kind word, a door left open. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Florence. The council where East and West signed a decree of reunion that began, let the heavens rejoice, and that the East did not receive. Today's word.
Your line: almost one. Today, if a reconciliation stalled, don't call it finished. Take one small step and leave the door open. Day seven hundred eighty.

781.hook: Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar, posts theses against the sale of indulgences
781.howItsDone: Catholics and Lutherans today hold joint services and dialogue about their shared history; in Catholic teaching indulgences still exist, but their sale is forbidden.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Florence, and a reunion signed but not received. Your line was almost one. Today a new split begins, this time inside the West. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

A preacher arrives near a small university town in Germany. He's raising money for the rebuilding of Saint Peter's in Rome, and he's offering indulgences to those who give. People cross the border to hear him. In that town, a friar of the Augustinian order, who teaches scripture at the university and hears confessions, is troubled by what his penitents are telling him. He sits down and writes a list of theses for debate. He's not trying to start a new church. He wants an argument about penance. Today's word is Reformation.
screen: `A PREACHER OFFERS INDULGENCES.` → `A FRIAR HEARS CONFESSIONS.` → `A LIST FOR DEBATE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. An indulgence, in Catholic teaching, is a remission of temporal punishment for sins already forgiven, granted by the Church. What troubled Martin Luther was the selling: the impression that a coin could do what only repentance and grace could. Next, his very first thesis. It goes back to Jesus. In Matthew, Jesus begins to preach, and in the Douay-Rheims he says, "Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Luther wrote that when Christ said this, he meant the whole life of believers to be one of penance. Not a transaction. A whole life turned around. Then, the door. The story often told is that he nailed the theses to the church door at Wittenberg. Some historians doubt the hammer. The list itself is not in doubt: he sent it to his archbishop, and printers spread it. Finally, what it became. Luther hoped for a debate. What followed was a break, deeper and longer than anyone at the time planned, with faults and hard words on more than one side. Today Catholics and Lutherans speak of this history together, and a pope has prayed alongside Lutheran leaders to remember it. Catholic tradition says the Church is always in need of purification, and the friar's first thesis was about exactly that: turning, every day. Hence the line for today, a monk wanted reform, though strictly he was a friar. The point holds. It began as a call to turn around.
screen: `AN INDULGENCE, AND ITS SALE.` · `THE WHOLE LIFE, PENANCE.` · `A DOOR, A LIST, A PRESS.` · `A DEBATE BECOMES A BREAK.` · then, large: `A MONK WANTED REFORM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Lutherans and Catholics together, or, if you don't pray, hold them in mind. Use the sit. Picture two churches on one street, one Catholic and one Lutheran, their bells ringing on the same Sunday. Hold both congregations in view: the families, the old people in the front pews, the children. Wish them both well, honestly and without picking. If you pray, you can use the prayer both say, the Our Father, slowly, once for each. The bell holds the time.
Reformation. The movement that began with a friar's call to reform the Church, and became a lasting division in the West. Today's word.
Your line: a monk wanted reform. Today, notice whether anything holy in your week has become a transaction, and turn it back toward the heart. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: What the reformers asked
782.hook: grace, scripture, and real abuses; Catholics today admit many of the abuses were real
782.howItsDone: Catholic and Protestant theologians continue to discuss grace, scripture and authority in formal dialogues; Catholic leaders have publicly acknowledged that abuses in the Church of that era were real.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Reformation began with a list for debate. Your line was a monk wanted reform. Today, what exactly did the reformers ask for? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A papal envoy stands before a German assembly with a message from the new pope, Adrian the Sixth. The assembly may have expected a defense. Instead, the envoy reads out a confession. The pope's instruction admits that for years there had been grave abuses in the Holy See itself, that the sickness had spread from the head to the members, and that the pope means to begin the cure at home. A pope, in the middle of the storm, saying: some of this is our fault. Today's title is a question: what the reformers asked.
screen: `AN ENVOY, A CONFESSION.` → `FROM THE HEAD TO THE MEMBERS.` → `WHAT DID THEY ASK?`

segments.voice: The reformers asked three kinds of things. First, grace. Luther read Paul's letter to the Romans, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just man liveth by faith." He came to believe we are made right with God by grace, received through faith, not earned. Catholics also teach that grace comes first and can't be bought. The real disagreements were about how grace works in a person, and those took longer to sort out. Second, scripture. The reformers wanted the Bible in ordinary people's hands and languages, and they held it to be the final rule over every church teaching. Catholics hold scripture and tradition together, read within the Church. That disagreement is real, and it's still discussed. Third, the abuses. This is where the reformers were often simply right. Some bishops drew income from dioceses they rarely saw. Church offices were bought and sold. Some priests had barely been taught. And indulgences had been marketed like a product. Pope Adrian's instruction said as much. So did Catholic reformers inside the Church, before and after Luther. Then, why it matters. It's possible to disagree with the reformers about grace or scripture and still say plainly: they saw real wounds. The Second Vatican Council said that for the separations, often enough, people on both sides were to blame. Honest reform can start with that kind of admission: the abuses were real.
screen: `FIRST: GRACE, NOT EARNED.` · `SECOND: SCRIPTURE IN EVERY HAND.` · `THIRD: THE ABUSES.` · `HONESTY BEFORE REFORM.` · then, large: `THE ABUSES WERE REAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a reform you need. Not one someone else needs. One in you. Use the sit. Let your week pass before you: what you said, what you spent, how you treated the people closest to you. Somewhere there's a habit that's drifted, the way an office drifts into a privilege. Don't fix it yet. Just name it, plainly, the way Pope Adrian's letter named the abuses. One sentence, said honestly to yourself. If you pray, you can bring that sentence before God. The bell holds the time.
Luther. The reformer who read Paul on grace, called for scripture in everyone's hands, and pointed to abuses the Church needed to face. Today's word.
Your line: the abuses were real. Today, when someone criticizes something you love, listen first for the part that's true before you defend the rest. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: The English break
783.hook: Henry VIII leaves Rome; Catholics and Protestants were both martyred in England
783.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps feast days for Saints Thomas More, John Fisher and the English martyrs; the Church of England also remembers its own martyrs of the period, and Catholics and Anglicans today meet in formal dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther: grace, scripture, and an end to real wrongs. Your line was the abuses were real. Today the break crosses the sea. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

Thomas More had been the king's friend, and then his Lord Chancellor. Now he's in the Tower of London, and all he has to do to walk out is swear an oath. Others around him have sworn. His own family begs him to. He's a lawyer; he knows every way around a sentence. He won't swear it. And he won't say why. Today's title is the English break, and it is a story where faithful people died on both sides.
screen: `THE KING'S FRIEND, IN THE TOWER.` → `ONE OATH FROM FREEDOM.` → `HE WON'T SWEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the break. King Henry the Eighth wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon declared invalid. The pope would not grant it. So the king and Parliament cut the English Church off from Rome and named the king its supreme head on earth. Next, the cost to Catholics. Oaths were required, and refusing put a person in the king's prisons. Thomas More refused, and so did John Fisher, a bishop. Both were tried for treason and beheaded. More is remembered as saying on the scaffold that he died the king's good servant, but God's first. The Catholic Church honors both as saints. Then, the turn. Henry had sent some Protestants to the fire too, but under his daughter Mary, a Catholic who restored ties to Rome, Protestants were burned for heresy in far greater numbers. Among them was Thomas Cranmer, the archbishop behind the English Book of Common Prayer. Anglicans remember him and others as martyrs. Under the next queen, Elizabeth, it turned again: Catholic priests were hanged, among them the Jesuit Edmund Campion, whom the Catholic Church honors as a saint. Last, what both sides shared. The words of the apostles in Acts could be said of every one of them; in the Douay-Rheims they read, "We ought to obey God, rather than men." They disagreed about what God asked. They agreed it was worth dying for. Catholics and Anglicans today can honor their own martyrs without pretending the others weren't sincere. Martyrs on both sides.
screen: `THE KING CUTS TIES WITH ROME.` · `MORE AND FISHER BEHEADED.` · `UNDER MARY, PROTESTANTS BURNED.` · `UNDER ELIZABETH, PRIESTS HANGED.` · then, large: `MARTYRS ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for all who died for conscience, or, if you don't pray, remember them. Use the sit. Bring to mind a few names from today: Thomas More, John Fisher, Thomas Cranmer, Edmund Campion. Hold them side by side, not as teams. Then widen it, to anyone anywhere who has suffered for refusing to say what they didn't believe. If you pray, you can commend them all to God's mercy, the ones you agree with and the ones you don't. The bell holds the time.
Thomas More. The king's chancellor who refused the oath of supremacy and was beheaded, one of many who died on both sides of England's break with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: martyrs on both sides. Today, when you meet someone whose convictions cross yours, look first for the sincerity, and honor it out loud if you can. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Trent opens, 1545
784.hook: a council that answers the reformers and reforms the Church from within
784.howItsDone: Catholics remember the Council of Trent as the center of the Catholic Reformation; religious orders founded or renewed in that era, like the Jesuits and the Discalced Carmelites, are still active today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas More. Your line was martyrs on both sides. This week went from Lateran IV and Constance to Florence, Luther's theses, the reformers' questions, and England. Now the Church answers. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Trent is a small city in a valley of the Alps, on the road between Italy and the German lands. That's why it was chosen: a place the emperor's people and the pope's people could both reach and both accept. For years, people on more than one side had called for a council. Popes hesitated, rulers quarreled, wars got in the way. At last the bishops gathered in the cathedral there. Today's word is Catholic Reformation.
screen: `A CITY IN THE ALPS.` → `YEARS OF WAITING.` → `AT LAST, A COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Historians sometimes call this the Counter-Reformation, as if it were only a reaction. Others prefer Catholic Reformation, because reform inside the Church had already started. Ignatius of Loyola, a wounded soldier, had gathered companions who became the Jesuits. Teresa of Avila would soon reform her Carmelite convents back toward poverty and prayer. Trent gathered that energy into one place. Next, the first big choice. The bishops at Trent decided to work on two things side by side: doctrine and discipline. They would answer the reformers' questions about faith, and at the same time fix the Church's own house. Not one or the other. Both. Then, what fixing the house meant. One example: the council insisted that bishops actually live in their dioceses and care for their people, instead of collecting income from far away. That was one of the abuses we heard about two days ago, addressed by the Church's own council. Last, the root. Paul writes in Romans, in the Douay-Rheims, "be reformed in the newness of your mind." In the Latin Bible the word is reformamini: be reformed. For Catholics, reform isn't someone else's word. It's in their own scripture, and it starts with the mind and the heart, not the walls: reform from within. Over the next days we'll follow what Trent actually said.
screen: `CATHOLIC REFORMATION, NOT JUST COUNTER.` · `DOCTRINE AND DISCIPLINE TOGETHER.` · `BISHOPS MUST LIVE WITH THEIR PEOPLE.` · `BE REFORMED IN YOUR MIND.` · then, large: `REFORM FROM WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reform one habit. Not your whole life. One habit. Use the sit. Go back to the reform you named a couple of days ago, or choose a fresh one. Picture the moment the habit usually happens: the time of day, the room, what's in your hand. Now picture yourself doing the better thing instead, once, in that same moment. Keep it small enough that you could actually do it tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for help to begin. The bell holds the time.
Catholic Reformation. The renewal of the Church from inside, gathered at the Council of Trent, answering the reformers and fixing its own house. Today's word.
Your line: reform from within. Today, before you ask anyone else to change, take the first step of your own one habit. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

fork.setup: you're a bishop at Trent's first sessions. some want only doctrine, some only reform. what do you choose?
options: doctrine only; the abuses can wait.
reform only; doctrine is settled.
work on both, side by side.
fork.reveal: the council decided to treat doctrine and discipline together: answer the questions and fix the house.

original.note: Latin: be reformed — Paul's word in Romans 12:2 in the Latin Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Catholic Church only fought back against the Reformation.
what it means: a renewal from inside, already underway, that Trent gathered: doctrine answered and discipline fixed together.
what a scholar hears: the debate over 'Counter-Reformation' versus 'Catholic Reformation', and Trent's decision to treat dogma and reform in parallel.
